title: Human body temperature reference — fever thresholds, per-site averages, care-seeking lines, hypothermia staging
description: Every row is one number that a named public-health or clinical source actually publishes, with the URL it was read from and a verbatim fragment. Deliberately excludes any band that no source publishes.

provenance.source: NHS — Fever in adults / Fever in children / Hypothermia / How to take your baby's temperature
provenance.note: All four NHS pages re-fetched from this machine on 2026-08-27 and returned HTTP 200 with the quoted strings present. Other NHS URLs used: /symptoms/fever-in-children/, /conditions/hypothermia/, /baby/health/how-to-take-your-babys-temperature/.

provenance.source: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) — Hypothermia (NBK545239) and Physiology, Fever (NBK562334)
provenance.note: Both chapters re-fetched 2026-08-27 (HTTP 200). NBK545239 is the source for the 35 °C hypothermia definition, the 36.5–37.5 °C normal range and the mild/moderate/severe staging. NBK562334 is the source for the low/moderate/high/hyperthermia fever bands and the per-site average readings.
Re-fetched 2026-08-27 (HTTP 200). Source for the 40 °C / 35 °C red flags and the 0.6 °C site offsets.

provenance.source: NICE CG65 — Hypothermia in the perioperative period (via NCBI Bookshelf NBK554181)
provenance.note: Re-fetched 2026-08-27 (HTTP 200). Source for the separate perioperative 'low core temperature' cut-off of 36.0 °C, which is NOT a definition of hypothermia.

provenance.source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Temperature management (paediatric guideline)
provenance.note: Re-fetched 2026-08-27 (HTTP 200). Source for the paediatric / neonatal low-temperature thresholds used in hospital care.

Quotes were captured by a manual read of these pages on 2026-08-27 and recorded in docs/数据来源核查-2026-08-27.md. Automated re-fetch of mayoclinic.org and cdc.gov from this build machine returns HTTP 403 (bot protection), so the numbers could not be re-verified by script — they are kept here only where they agree with a machine-verified source above.

provenance.source: PMC6456186 — systematic review of normal body temperature values (9,227 measurements)
provenance.note: Re-fetched 2026-08-27 (HTTP 200). Used to cross-check the per-site averages published in StatPearls NBK562334; the two agree.

Rows carry a "setting" value (home | hospital | reference | device) and an "audience" value (any | adult | child | infant | neonate). The lookup endpoint applies only home rows unless you pass ?setting=all, and ?person= narrows by age group, so a home reader is never shown an inpatient escalation threshold or another age group's cut-off.

columns.label: Audience
columns.note: any | adult | child | infant | neonate — pass ?person= to filter

columns.label: Setting
columns.note: home | hospital | reference | device — which context the row applies in

columns.label: Rule
columns.note: range | gte | lte | offset | duration | sign

columns.label: What it means / what to do

rows.label: Normal range 36.5–37.5 °C (97.7–99.5 °F)
rows.action: Within the range StatPearls gives for a normal value.
rows.quote: The normal value ranges from 36.5 °C to 37.5 °C.
rows.note: °F values are the exact conversions; the source publishes °C only.

rows.label: About 36.4 °C (97.5 °F)
rows.action: NHS describes this as a normal temperature in babies and children; it can vary slightly.
rows.source: NHS — How to take your baby's temperature
rows.quote: A normal temperature in babies and children is about 36.4C, but this can vary slightly.
rows.note: NHS does not publish a normal range for adults; it only says normal temperature differs per person and changes during the day.

rows.label: Mean 36.57 °C; mean ± 2 SD 35.73–37.41 °C
rows.action: Use the interval, not 37.0, when judging whether a single oral reading is unusual.
rows.quote: oral is 36.57 degrees C (97.83 degrees F)
rows.note: c_min/c_max are mean ± 2 SD from the underlying review; the mean is in the label.

rows.label: Mean 37.04 °C; mean ± 2 SD 36.32–37.76 °C
rows.action: Rectal readings run higher than oral ones; do not apply an oral threshold to them.
rows.source: PMC6456186 — systematic review of normal body temperature
rows.quote: rectal mean 37.04 °C

rows.label: Mean 36.64 °C; mean ± 2 SD 35.76–37.52 °C
rows.action: Measured mean is close to the oral mean, despite the '+0.6 °C' rule of thumb in some handbooks.
rows.quote: tympanic is 36.64 degrees C (97.95 degrees F)
rows.note: Where the 'ear = oral + 0.6 °C' shortcut and the measured means disagree, this dataset keeps both and says so.

rows.label: Mean 35.97 °C; mean ± 2 SD 35.01–36.93 °C
rows.action: A healthy adult armpit reading can legitimately be below 36 °C — so 'under 36' is not hypothermia.
rows.quote: The average axillary temperature reading is 35.97 degrees C (96.75 degrees F)
rows.note: This row is the reason the dataset does not define a 36 °C hypothermia line.

rows.label: +0.6 °C (1.0 °F) vs oral
rows.action: Add roughly 0.6 °C to an oral fever threshold when reading rectally.
rows.quote: Rectal and tympanic membrane temperatures are about 0.6 °C higher than oral temperatures, whereas skin temperatures are about 0.6 °C lower.
rows.note: Merck gives one number (0.6 °C), not a 0.3–0.6 °C range; some patient leaflets give the range.

rows.label: +0.6 °C (1.0 °F) vs oral
rows.action: Treat an ear reading as about 0.6 °C above an oral one, but expect wider scatter.
rows.quote: Rectal and tympanic membrane temperatures are about 0.6 °C higher than oral temperatures
rows.note: The measured means in this dataset put ear and oral within 0.1 °C of each other — the two statements come from different kinds of source.

rows.label: −0.6 °C (1.0 °F) vs oral
rows.action: Forehead and skin readings run low; Merck calls crystal/skin monitoring insensitive and not recommended for this purpose.
rows.quote: whereas skin temperatures are about 0.6 °C lower
rows.note: NHS additionally warns that some infrared forehead devices do not meet UK regulations.

rows.label: 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or higher = fever
rows.action: The public-health line most UK services use when telling you to act.
rows.quote: A high temperature is usually considered to be 38C or above. This is sometimes called a fever.
rows.note: NHS publishes °C only; 100.4 °F is the exact conversion.

rows.label: Low-grade 37.3–38.0 °C (99.1–100.4 °F)
rows.action: Clinically a fever band; not a 'call a doctor' threshold on its own.
rows.quote: Low-grade: 37.3 to 38.0 C (99.1 to 100.4 F)
rows.note: Published fever bands are not the same cut-offs as the NHS/Mayo advice lines; both are in this dataset, each labelled.

rows.label: Moderate-grade 38.1–39.0 °C (100.6–102.2 °F)
rows.action: Usually tolerated by a healthy adult; rest and fluids, watch the trend.
rows.quote: Moderate-grade: 38.1 to 39.0 C (100.6 to 102.2 F)

rows.label: High-grade 39.1–41.0 °C (102.4–105.8 °F)
rows.action: High-grade band in the clinical literature.
rows.quote: High-grade: 39.1 to 41 C (102.4 to 105.8 F)

rows.label: Above 41.0 °C (105.8 °F)
rows.action: StatPearls: hyperthermia/hyperpyrexia band — uncontrolled rise above the set-point; emergency.
rows.quote: Hyperthermia: Greater than 41 C (105.8 F)
rows.note: Cleveland Clinic defines hyperpyrexia as above 106.7 °F (41.5 °C); the two cut-offs differ and both exist in the literature.

rows.label: Above 40.0 °C (104.0 °F) — or below 35.0 °C (95.0 °F)
rows.action: Merck lists this as a red flag requiring immediate assessment.
rows.quote: Temperature > 40° C or < 35° C

rows.label: 38.0 °C (100.4 °F) or higher → seek care immediately
rows.action: Do not wait for the fever to come down on your own; contact emergency services / go to A&E or the ER.
rows.quote: is under 3 months old and has a temperature of 38C or higher
rows.note: AAP, Mayo Clinic and CDC publish the same 38.0 °C / 100.4 °F line for this age group; only the contact route differs (111 vs paediatrician vs ER).

rows.label: 39.0 °C (102.2 °F) or higher → contact a clinician the same day
rows.action: NHS uses the 39 °C line specifically for the 3–6 month age band.
rows.quote: is 3 to 6 months old and has a temperature of 39C or higher
rows.note: There is no single published 'children over 39 °C' rule: NHS ties 39 °C to 3–6 months, AAP uses 40 °C (104 °F), Mayo uses 38.9 °C (102 °F) rectal for 3–6 months.

rows.label: 39.4 °C (103 °F) or higher → call your health care provider
rows.action: Mayo's adult number. NHS gives no adult temperature cut-off at all.
rows.source: Mayo Clinic — Fever (symptoms and when to see a doctor)
rows.quote: Call your health care provider if your temperature is 103 F (39.4 C) or higher.
rows.note: US-style triage line; the page could not be re-fetched by script (403) — see provenance.

rows.label: Fever lasting more than 3 days → see a clinician
rows.action: Duration triggers care independently of the number on the thermometer.
rows.quote: stays at 103 F (39.4 C) or higher or lasts longer than three days
rows.note: Other published durations: NHS (children) 5 days; Merck 24–48 h for a phone call and 3–4 days for a visit. No single duration is universally agreed.

rows.label: Fever lasting 5 days or more → see a clinician
rows.action: NHS threshold for children; also contact NHS 111 if the child is getting worse or you are worried.
rows.quote: lasted for 5 days or more
rows.note: AAP uses more than 24 h under 2 years and more than 72 h at 2 years and over; Mayo uses 3 days.

rows.label: Below 35.0 °C (95.0 °F) → hypothermia, medical emergency
rows.action: Call emergency services. Handle the person gently and keep them warm while help is on the way.
rows.source: StatPearls — Hypothermia; NHS — Hypothermia; CDC — Winter weather
rows.quote: Hypothermia is defined as a decrease in body temperature below 35 °C.
rows.note: NHS: 'a dangerous drop in body temperature below 35C … It's a medical emergency'. CDC and Mayo use the same 95 °F / 35 °C line.

rows.label: Mild hypothermia 32.0–35.0 °C (90–95 °F)
rows.action: Shivering, cognitive impairment; passive external rewarming is often sufficient in alert, stable patients.
rows.quote: Patients with mild hypothermia have a core body temperature ranging from 32 to 35 °C (90 to 95 °F).
rows.note: Clinical staging for hospital care — not a home-triage tool.

rows.label: Moderate hypothermia 28.0–32.0 °C (82–90 °F)
rows.action: Cognitive decline and lethargy; active rewarming under medical care.
rows.quote: Patients with moderate hypothermia have a core body temperature of 28 to 32 °C (82-90 °F).

rows.label: Severe hypothermia below 28.0 °C (82.0 °F)
rows.action: Risk of ventricular arrhythmias; hospital-level rewarming (up to ECMO / bypass).
rows.quote: Individuals with severe hypothermia have a core body temperature of less than 28 °C (82 °F).

rows.label: 35.0–36.5 °C (95.0–97.7 °F) → below the usual range, not hypothermia
rows.action: Recheck after 10 minutes, keep warm, and seek care if there are symptoms or the reading keeps falling.
rows.source: Derived: StatPearls hypothermia definition + measured axillary means
rows.quote: The average axillary temperature reading is 35.97 degrees C
rows.note: No public-health source defines hypothermia at 36 °C, and the measured axillary mean in healthy adults is 35.97 °C — a 35.9 °C armpit reading is not a diagnosis.

rows.label: Perioperative: core temperature below 36.0 °C is 'low' and needs active management
rows.action: This is a hospital quality threshold, not a layperson's hypothermia threshold.
rows.source: NICE CG65 — Hypothermia: prevention and management in adults having surgery
rows.quote: core temperature below 36.0°C
rows.note: Included because this is where the widely-copied '36 °C = hypothermia' claim seems to come from.

rows.label: Paediatric inpatient: below 36.0 °C is treated as low temperature; neonates below 36.5 °C
rows.action: Hospital escalation thresholds for children under inpatient care.
rows.source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Temperature management
rows.quote: paediatric low temperature (or hypothermia) <36 °C … neonates <36.5 °C
rows.note: Some NHS 111 regional triage pages likewise list 'temperature below 36 °C' as a sign to assess — the number is a care trigger in those settings, still not the definition.

rows.label: Newborn below 36.5 °C (97.7 °F) → warm and get help
rows.action: Neonates are managed far more strictly than older children for cold readings.
rows.source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Temperature management
rows.quote: neonates <36.5 °C
rows.note: This is the one place where a threshold above 35 °C is genuinely the right safety line.

rows.label: Rash that does not fade under a glass
rows.action: Emergency — call 999 / go to A&E, do not wait for the temperature to change.
rows.quote: rash that does not fade when you press a glass against it
rows.note: Emergency signs are listed without a temperature because no temperature is required to act.

rows.label: Stiff neck, dislike of bright light, severe headache
rows.action: Emergency — these are the meningeal signs both NHS and Mayo list alongside fever.
rows.source: NHS — Fever in children; Mayo Clinic — Fever symptoms
rows.quote: stiff neck and pain when you bend your head forward
rows.note: Quote is from Mayo's adult list; NHS lists 'stiff neck' and 'bothered by light' for children.

rows.label: A fit (febrile seizure) for the first time, or a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
rows.action: Emergency. NHS lists a first fit as a 999/A&E sign; Mayo says call 911 if a seizure lasts more than 5 minutes or recovery is not quick.
rows.source: NHS — Fever in children; Mayo Clinic — First aid: fever
rows.quote: having a fit (febrile seizure) for the first time

rows.label: Blue / grey / pale / blotchy skin, cold hands and feet, drowsy and hard to wake
rows.action: Emergency — circulatory and consciousness signs outrank the thermometer reading.
rows.quote: skin colour changes (blue/grey/pale/blotchy)
rows.note: NHS also lists unusually cold hands and feet and being extremely agitated or confused in the same block.

rows.label: Difficulty breathing, breathlessness, breathing very fast, or chest pain
rows.action: Emergency.
rows.source: NHS — Fever in children; Mayo Clinic — Fever symptoms
rows.quote: difficulty breathing / breathlessness / breathing very fast

rows.label: Digital thermometer should reset below 35 °C (95 °F) before each reading
rows.action: Practical check that the device can actually read the range that matters.
rows.quote: Before each new measurement with a digital thermometer, the device should be reset to below 35 C (95 F).

notes: Two families of numbers are mixed in everyday life and kept separate here: clinical fever bands (StatPearls: 37.3 / 38.1 / 39.1 / 41 °C) and public-health advice lines (NHS 38 °C, Mayo 39.4 °C). Neither is wrong; they answer different questions.

Hypothermia is defined below 35.0 °C (95.0 °F) by NHS, CDC, Mayo and StatPearls. The widely-copied 'below 36 °C' line comes from hospital settings (NICE perioperative, paediatric inpatient escalation), not from the definition.
Site offsets are approximations from Merck (±0.6 °C). Where a source publishes a per-site fever threshold instead (Mayo: axillary 37.2 °C / 99 °F), the threshold is preferable to the offset.

No source in this dataset publishes a four-level 'slightly elevated / low-grade / moderate / high' chart with the boundaries usually seen on conversion websites. Those boundaries are editorial, so they are not in this file.
Fever thresholds differ by measurement site. Applying the 38.0 °C oral line to an axillary reading over-reads; applying it to a rectal reading under-reads by roughly 0.6 °C.
disclaimer: Reference data transcribed from published sources on 2026-08-27. Not medical advice and not a diagnosis. Care-seeking rules differ by country, by age and by the person's underlying health; when in doubt, contact a clinician or emergency services. If any number here matters to a decision, open the source URL and read it yourself.
